issues.legal_issue: A pending special-leave proceeding under the Constitution survives the repeal of the governing rent-control law when the replacement law does not clearly terminate that constitutional review.
material_facts: The eviction proceeding had been initiated under the former rent-control law, and a High Court revision had resulted in an eviction order before the tenant sought special leave to appeal.
While the special-leave proceeding was pending, the former rent-control law was repealed and a replacement rent-control law came into force.
The premises were outside the replacement law's coverage because their non-residential area exceeded the statutory threshold.

The replacement law provided for abatement of certain pending proceedings concerning premises outside its coverage, but did not clearly direct that a pending proceeding under the Supreme Court's constitutional jurisdiction should abate.
issues.conclusion: The proceeding under Article 136 survived and could be decided on its merits; it did not abate under the replacement law.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 69 and 70 of the Karnataka Rent Act, 1999 govern the transfer, continuation, and abatement of proceedings following repeal of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961. Section 70(2)(c) applies to specified proceedings concerning premises outside the new Act's coverage, while Section 70(3) preserves the residual operation of Sections 6, 8, and 24 of the Karnataka General Clauses Act, 1899. Abatement must be strictly construed and applies only where its reach is clear; absent a contrary legislative intention, it terminates proceedings pending at the relevant stage, not an original case already adjudicated below and reopened for review by a superior forum. Article 136 confers plenary constitutional jurisdiction that subordinate legislation cannot curtail. The Court relied on Durga Shankar Mehta v. Thakur Raghuraj Singh, Union Carbide Corporation v. Union of India, S.P. Sampath Kumar v. Union of India, Surya Dev Rai v. Ram Chander Rai, and Gyan Chand v. Kunjbeharilal; it distinguished Ram Adhar Singh v. Ramroop Singh, Chattar Singh v. Thakur Prasad Singh, Satyanarayan Prasad Sah v. State of Bihar, and Mst. Bibi Rahmani Khatoon v. Harkoo Gope, which concerned legislation that abated the original case itself.

rule.if: local_rent_law_repealed_during_review and premises_outside_replacement_rent_regime and article_136_special_leave_review and lower_court_eviction_case_already_adjudicated and no_clear_direction_to_abate_constitutional_review

predicates.local_rent_law_repealed_during_review: A local rent-control law was repealed while a challenge to a decision under that law remained pending.
predicates.premises_outside_replacement_rent_regime: The premises fell outside the coverage of the replacement rent-control regime.
predicates.article_136_special_leave_review: The pending matter was a discretionary special-leave review under the Supreme Court's constitutional jurisdiction, rather than an ordinary appeal as of right.
predicates.lower_court_eviction_case_already_adjudi: The eviction claim had already been adjudicated below, and the pending matter concerned review of that adjudication.
predicates.no_clear_direction_to_abate_constitution: The replacement law did not clearly direct, expressly or by necessary implication, that the pending constitutional review be terminated.
predicates.constitutional_review_survives: The pending constitutional review continues and may be decided on its merits.

issues.definition: When a local rent-control law is repealed during a constitutional special-leave review of an already adjudicated eviction claim concerning premises outside the replacement regime, and the replacement law does not clearly terminate that review, the review survives.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant's participation with family members in a partnership operating the existing business in the rented premises does not establish unlawful subletting without proof that the tenant parted with legal possession or the right to enjoy the premises.
material_facts: The premises had been rented for a business that continued to operate there after the business was converted from a sole proprietorship to a partnership.
The tenant joined the partnership with family members, including brothers, a brother's wife, and a cousin.
The tenant's family was joint, depended on the business for its livelihood, and included sixteen members.
There was no evidence that the tenant withdrew from the business, that the partners alone carried it on, or that the partners had exclusive possession of the premises.
There was no evidence that the partnership was a device concealing a transfer of possession or the right to use the premises.
issues.conclusion: The landlord did not establish unlawful subletting under Section 21(1)(f) of the former Act; the eviction ground was not made out, and the eviction proceedings were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21(1)(f) of the Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961 covers unlawful subletting of all or part of the premises and assignment or transfer of the tenant's interest in another manner. Under Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease entails a transfer of the right to enjoy property, and parting with that right is essential to a sub-lease. The landlord bears the burden of proving subletting; prima facie proof that another occupant has exclusive possession for valuable consideration may discharge that burden and call for rebuttal. A change in the constitution of a partnership, or the tenant's entry into partnership to conduct business on the premises, does not alone establish subletting while the tenant retains legal possession. The court may look past a partnership arrangement if it conceals a transfer of possession or the right to use the premises. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. S.B. Sardar Ranjit Singh, Krishnawati v. Hans Raj, Murlidhar v. Chuni Lal, Helper Girdharbhai v. Saiyed Mohmad Mirasaheb Kadri, and Parvinder Singh v. Renu Gautam.

rule.if: eviction_claim_based_on_unlawful_subletting and partnership_operates_in_tenanted_premises and tenant_actively_participates_in_business and tenant_retains_legal_possession and no_evidence_of_partners_exclusive_possession_or_concealed_transfer

predicates.eviction_claim_based_on_unlawful_sublett: The landlord sought eviction on the basis that the tenant had unlawfully sublet or transferred an interest in the premises.
predicates.partnership_operates_in_tenanted_premise: A partnership conducted business in the premises that had been rented to the tenant.
predicates.tenant_actively_participates_in_business: The tenant remained associated with the partnership's business activity in the premises.
predicates.tenant_retains_legal_possession: The tenant retained legal possession or control of the premises rather than parting with the right to enjoy them.
predicates.no_evidence_of_partners_exclusive_posses: There was no evidence that the partners had exclusive possession or that the partnership concealed a transfer of possession or the right to use the premises.

issues.definition: When an eviction claim based on unlawful subletting concerns a partnership business in rented premises, the tenant remains active and retains legal possession, and there is no evidence of exclusive possession by the partners or a concealed transfer, the subletting ground is not established.
